title: Review of c27's ringswim repair claim on fresh seeds 11 and 12: 4/4 front-cut cells re-close their link ring by +120 against exact twins; seed 11 cell 22 then swims 3.99 body lengths with the ring held; one cell below the claimed 0.26 closure threshold also recovered
summary: c27's twinrepair.py, unchanged, at T0=10000 for 2000 steps: seed 11 with the wound substrate kept (KEEP_S, as seeds 3-8) and seed 12 with the wound reset to bath (world.damage, as seeds 0-1), 2 cells each; plus a labkit run of seed 11 with --damage 200:0.4:half. All 4 cut cells (40% of area, 47-52% of their links erased) re-close their ring from closure 0.19-0.56 to >= 0.9 at +120 and keep a ring score >= 1.5 in every frame of the second half. Seed 11 cell 22 (251 px): after the cut it rounds into a compact ringed cell by +320 and moves 3.99 body lengths by +2000 (its twin 1.2), ending at 174 px (69% of its pre-cut area; twin 253). Seed 11 cell 23 ends at 222 px, the same as its twin. Seed 12 cell 15 repairs and is then lost at +1440, as its twin is at +1300. Seed 12 cell 39 was left with closure 0.19, below the 0.26 that c27 found lethal, yet re-closed by +120 and ended at 544 px (larger than its 299 px start, so it probably absorbed a neighbour), while its twin was lost at +640. labkit's generic damage follow-up cannot separate repair from merging here: the cut cell merged with another at t=11050 and the comparator at 10050.

pass: 2/2 re-close (wound reset to bath); one is lost at +1440 like its twin; one recovers from closure 0.19, apparently by absorbing a neighbour

verdicts.limitation: 4 cuts on 2 seeds. Area recovery is partial (cell 22 ends at 69% of its pre-cut area, while cell 23 matches its twin), and the cells' areas swing through divisions and mergers in both arms, so 'regains pre-cut area' is not a clean test. The 0.26 closure threshold for death is contradicted once (cell 39, closure 0.19, recovered, probably via a merger). Curvature flow of the phase field helps the shape repair by construction; the ring re-closure is the cell's own chemistry.
